analysis.one_liner: Shortens brand-name biologic drug market exclusivity from 12 years to 7 years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let cheaper biosimilar copies of biologic drugs reach the market five years sooner, never got a vote — it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs are complex medicines made from living cells, and the law lets the original brand keep competitors off the market for 12 years after approval. This bill would cut that window to 7 years, letting lower-priced "biosimilar" copies arrive five years earlier — but only for drugs approved after the bill became law. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who pay for biologic drugs, including through Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance. Biosimilar competition typically brings prices down substantially, so reaching the market five years earlier means lower costs and earlier access. Biosimilar manufacturers would also gain a larger market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying for expensive biologic drugs

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the marketing exclusivity period for brand-name biological products from 12 years to 7 years, so competing biosimilars could be licensed and marketed five years sooner.
Applies only to biological products whose reference product is licensed on or after enactment, so it does not disturb exclusivity already granted for drugs on the market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug manufacturers, who would lose five years of sales without biosimilar competition on future drugs, and whose revenue from those products would fall once cheaper copies enter. Some future research investment could shift as a result.

drawbacks.text: The core trade-off is real: the 12-year exclusivity window exists to reward companies for the large, risky investment of developing biologic medicines, and cutting it to 7 years would reduce the revenue that supports that investment, which industry argues could mean fewer new biologics in the future.

The bill applies only to drugs licensed after enactment, so it would deliver no relief on any biologic already approved or in the approval pipeline at the time — patients taking today's high-cost biologics would see no change for many years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and well documented: longer exclusivity periods for biologics keep cheaper biosimilars off the market, and shortening the window transfers savings to patients and payers. The cost — possibly slower development of some future biologics — is genuine but speculative, and the bill's gradual application would have let researchers adjust. On balance the savings to consumers and taxpayers are large relative to the uncertain innovation cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the PRICED Act on June 23, 2016, with four original cosponsors, to cut brand-name biologic exclusivity from 12 years to 7.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, which is where its action history ends.
The bill ended the 114th Congress with no committee action, no floor vote, and no companion progress, so its exclusivity change was never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers kept the full 12 years of market exclusivity for new drugs, and patients kept paying brand prices for years longer than the bill would have allowed.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PRICED Act to shorten biologic exclusivity from 12 years to 7.

for.name: Reps. Elijah Cummings, Jim McDermott, Lloyd Doggett, and Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 8 additional House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors who signed on after introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 8 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over drug regulation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 23, 2016 and never reported the bill out or scheduled any action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, controlled the committee's agenda and did not schedule a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that blocked action was chaired by a Republican; the bill never reached a recorded vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would cut five years off their exclusive sales window for future biologic drugs, during which they face no biosimilar competition. The committee's failure to act preserved the status quo.
A shorter exclusivity window would open the market to biosimilar competitors five years earlier, letting them sell lower-priced copies of future biologics sooner.
